look_here_first: TEXAS BLUEGRASS — a native state-level rhizomatous cool-season PERENNIAL, usually flowering in spring with pale to woolly-looking heads on taller culms. Unlike introduced Poa annua, Texas bluegrass is DIOECIOUS: staminate and pistillate plants are separate, and female florets usually have particularly long cobwebby HAIRS arising around basal lemma/callus; male flowers can also bear sparser hairs. The one archived landscape photograph shows prominent pale flowering heads, not a confirmed female floret, pistil, web tuft, rhizome or Hays voucher. A correct determination requires true reproductive macro plus documented rhizome.

best_field_traits: Perennial spreading on underground rhizomes forming prairie grass sod, often 20–70 cm high.
Dioecious: male and female florets on separate individuals.
Female spikelets have strongly woolly/cobwebby basal lemma hair tufts; 20× image essential.
Bright to pale silver flowering heads in spring and smooth sheaths.
Boat-shaped blade tips and a membranous true ligule are genus-level characteristics.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Texas bluegrass connected rhizome linking at least two live shoots in one legal specimen
Individually determined male and female panicles photographed separately with source verification; show florets and functional anthers/pistils
20×-40× dorsal FEMALE lemma base showing actual cobwebby hair tufts and three-plus-two nerves, mm ruler
Male counterpart lemma base and sexual organs under same scale to avoid an overstrong 'hairless male' rule
Same-plant true leaf collar and boat-shaped blade tip, both genus-level
crew_field_check: Start with the current Texas bluegrass field photo: pale feathery mature panicles on upright stems; no tiny lemma hairs are directly visible.
Locate same-plant underground connected RHIZOMES; do not mistake clump density or independent tussocks for a traced rhizome.
Sample male and female plants in bloom and confirm actual unisexual reproductive structures at magnification; source label alone does not prove sex.
Separate a mature female floret and image actual basal webby lemma hairs; these are microscopic-level proof not available in any present learner photograph.
Compare rhizomatous but bisexual P. pratensis and low normally bisexual P. annua before committing a native/habitat/range decision. Preserve unreviewed county status.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Both P. annua and Texas bluegrass have a membranous ligule and boat-shaped blade tips, so neither clue identifies the native species. Compare reproductive SEX on individually collected florets and actual connected underground rhizomes on same-plant clumps. Kentucky bluegrass (P. pratensis) can also be rhizomatous and may have some basal lemma hairs; its flowers are bisexual, so woolliness alone does not prove P. arachnifera.
not_reliable_alone: Boat-shaped grass leaf tip is a genus trait common to both Poa species
One very green or woolly head photographed at a distance, without sex/lemma macro
Ligule without the complete rooted specimen
Treating state native range as a Hays county voucher

visual_comparison.title: Poa arachnifera — annual introduced vs perennial dioecious Texas bluegrass
visual_comparison.subtitle: Two original and two newly licensed source photos. Annual has direct photographed boat-tip/ligule references; Texas flowering stand remains at gross-scale only. Source-only identification retained.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: BOAT TIP + LIGULE = POA GENUS. P. ANNUA = usually annual and bisexual; P. ARACHNIFERA = perennial rhizomes and separate SEXES with WEBBY female lemma bases.

items.label: Texas bluegrass — original source photo
items.image_role: Actually visually inspected local JPEG; taxon determination from original source
items.caption: Wide field photo shows many pale fuzzy-looking panicles and flowering culms. Individual female cobwebby lemma hairs and sexual organs are NOT visible enough to verify.
items.why_it_matters: Native TEXAS BLUEGRASS is a rhizomatous sod-forming cool-season PERENNIAL, dioecious with male and female plants. Female spikelet florets have conspicuous cobwebby long hairs at basal lemmas that make whole flowering heads look woolly. A distant fuzzy head is only a clue: a verified female floret macro and rooted rhizomes are needed.
items.creator: ctchristorres
items.photo_status: STRUCTURES VISIBLE: panicle/leaf/stem level only. No actual rootstock or individual floret/ligule physically confirmed.

items.label: Annual bluegrass — original source photo
items.image_role: Actually visually inspected local JPEG; taxon determination from original source
items.caption: Whole plant photo shows low flowering grass, green leaves, and flowering branches. Neither microscopic lemma characters nor ligule is resolvable.
items.why_it_matters: INTRODUCED annual bluegrass: soft low light-green grass in lawns and paths with small open pale green panicles; folded emerging blades with boat-prow tips and a translucent short membranous ligule. Usually annual, though persistent biotypes occur. True flowers are generally bisexual, unlike dioecious Texas bluegrass.
items.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)
items.photo_status: STRUCTURES VISIBLE: panicle/leaf/stem level only. No actual rootstock or individual floret/ligule physically confirmed.

items.label: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — boat-prow shaped leaf tip
items.image_role: Flickr/Commons macro photographed in Pasadena at 30×, identified by original photographer as annual bluegrass; illustrates the boat-shaped folded grass leaf TIP, shared by other Poa, not a species diagnostic.
items.caption: The green blade narrows to a blunt folded, keel-like 'prow' tip. The lightened very tip is visible; it may be a worn or dry margin, not a separate auricle. The photographer reported magnification 30×, but supplied no calibrated ruler. This proves the shared Poa leaf tip shape, not annual versus Texas bluegrass.
items.why_it_matters: This is an actual photograph of the genus recognition clue that the former whole-plant picture could not resolve. The tip belongs to Poa annua per source label, but its shape alone never distinguishes P. annua from Texas bluegrass.
items.creator: Jason Hollinger
items.photo_status: Source-credited physically viewed licensed 600×530 Commons photo on 2026-10-21. Source identification not independently voucher-confirmed. General Poa-only character, no ruler or unseen hairs.

items.label: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — actual membranous ligule and blade/sheath collar
items.image_role: Four-view composite macro of one Austrian source-identified annual-bluegrass blade/sheath junction, with original photographer's genuine 10 mm scale, NOT four individuals.
items.caption: Four source-photo views show the same kind of grass blade/sheath collar. The bottom view exposes the whitish membranous flap (ligule) exactly where green blade separates from the upper sheath. The genuine 10-mm photo scale sits at bottom; do not confuse the entire pale sheath with the ligule or infer its precise size without local measurement.
items.why_it_matters: Teaches the actual part crews must photograph: a thin membranous ligule at the junction, not a tuft of hairs or a leaf tip. Texas bluegrass also has a membranous ligule; the difference lies primarily in reproductive sex and perennial rhizomes.
items.creator: Stefan.lefnaer
items.photo_status: Commons 960×1277 composite photographed in Vienna, exact source and CC BY-SA 4.0 visually verified 2026-10-21; only clearly visible pale membrane and collar marked. Four views of anatomy, not four independent specimens.

visual_comparison.overlay_note: Four actual credited photo panels; original CC BY 2.0 and CC BY-NC source rights retained and two Commons CC BY / CC BY-SA anatomy closeups linked externally for provisional user review. NO current Texas-bluegrass female lemmas or rhizomes photographed; don't label broad white heads 'female webs'. 10 mm scale remains photographer's, do not claim precise ligule dimension.
